questions.q: Which of these is a logic error?
questions.explain: A logic error is valid code that runs to the end and produces the wrong answer. There is no error message to read, so you find it by predicting and tracing.
options: A missing closing bracket that stops the file from running
A discount function that runs without complaint but gives 5% where it should give 10%
A program that runs out of memory

questions.q: You traced a loop and compared each row with your prediction. Rows 1 to 4 match, rows 5 and 6 do not. Where do you look first?
questions.explain: Once a value goes wrong, everything computed from it goes wrong too. Row 6 may only be wrong because row 5 was. The first disagreement is closest to the cause.
options: At row 6, the last wrong one
At row 5 and the step just before it: the first place where the trace and the prediction disagree
At row 1, because bugs are always at the start
Anywhere: all wrong rows are equally useful

questions.q: A report is wrong for a shop with 12,000 orders. Why is it worth finding a list of 3 or 4 orders that shows the same bug?
questions.explain: A trace table of 12,000 rows is useless. With the smallest input that still shows the bug, every step fits on paper and the first wrong step is easy to spot.
options: Because JavaScript runs faster on small lists
Because you can predict and trace a small input by hand, row by row
Because the bug only exists for small inputs
Because tests may not use large lists

questions.q: Why is "change things until the output looks right" a poor way to fix a logic error?
questions.explain: Changing === to >= made the invoice example "work" by luck, while other amounts still failed. A fix should come from an explanation of the cause, proven by a test that failed before.
options: It takes too long to type
It can hide the bug for this input while leaving the cause in place for others
JavaScript does not allow code to be changed after it runs
It always makes the program slower

questions.q: A loop is for (let i = 0; i <= list.length; i++) and adds up list[i]. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Positions run from 0 to length − 1. With <= the loop makes one extra step past the end, and number + undefined is NaN.
options: The last step reads list[list.length], which is undefined, so the total becomes NaN
Nothing: <= and < behave the same here

questions.q: A hotel serves breakfast every day from the 3rd to the 7th of the month, both days included. How many breakfasts?
questions.explain: 7 − 3 = 4 counts the gaps between days, not the days. With both ends included you need one more: 7 − 3 + 1 = 5. This is the fencepost error.

questions.q: A 30-metre fence has a post every 3 metres, including one at each end. How many posts?
questions.explain: There are 30 / 3 = 10 gaps, and one more post than gaps because both ends have a post. Counting gaps when you meant items (or the reverse) is the classic off-by-one.

questions.q: Which return in this function can never run?
questions.explain: The second line is only reached when the weight is 1 kg or less, and none of those weights is over 10 kg. Ask "which inputs reach this line?" for each line; an empty answer means dead code.

questions.q: A function has several overlapping checks like total >= 5000000 and total >= 1000000, each returning straight away. In what order should they go?
questions.explain: Every total over ₦50,000 is also over ₦10,000. If the broader check comes first, it catches everything and the specific rule is unreachable.
options: Highest threshold first, so the most specific rule gets its chance before the broader one
Alphabetical order of the discount names

questions.q: Why does this crash for canCheckout(null), even though it checks for null?
questions.explain: A check that makes a later line safe must come before that line. Reading a property of null throws a TypeError, so the protecting check never gets a chance.
options: Because user.banned is read before the null check runs
Because the function has three returns
Because null is not allowed as an argument

questions.q: In a recursive function, what is the base case?
questions.explain: Recursion solves a problem through a smaller version of itself. The base case is the smallest version, answered directly. Without one that every input reaches, the calls never stop.
options: The first line of the function
The case the function answers directly, without calling itself, so the chain of calls can stop
The largest input the function accepts
The default value of a parameter

questions.q: What does "RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded" usually tell you?
questions.explain: Each call waits for the inner one, and waiting calls pile up. When there are too many, JavaScript stops the program. Look for a missing or unreachable base case.
options: A list is too long to loop over
A function kept calling itself (directly or through others) and never reached a stopping point
The computer is out of disk space

questions.q: function sumTo(n) { if (n === 0) return 0; return n + sumTo(n - 1); } works for 5. Which call never stops?
questions.explain: 2.5, 1.5, 0.5, −0.5, … skips over 0, so n === 0 is never true. A base case of n <= 0 is reachable from every number.

questions.q: Why does the fixed founder function keep a visited set of users?
questions.explain: With a cycle the chain never reaches null. Remembering who has been visited gives the function another way out: if a user comes round again, report the broken data instead of looping forever.
options: To make the function faster on long chains
To count how many users there are
So that a cycle in the data (A referred by B, B referred by A) is noticed and the recursion stops

questions.q: Removing cancelled orders with splice inside a forward loop leaves one behind "only sometimes". When?
questions.explain: After a removal, the next order slides into the position the loop just checked, and the loop moves on. The skipped order only matters when it is also cancelled, which happens when two are adjacent.
options: When the list has an odd number of orders
When two cancelled orders are next to each other
When the first order is cancelled
When there are no cancelled orders

questions.q: What is the simplest reliable fix for removing items from a list while looping over it?
questions.explain: If the list you are walking through never changes, the loop and the list cannot disagree. (Walking backwards also works when you must change the list in place; i++ after a removal would make things worse.)
options: Do not change that list: build a new list of the items to keep

questions.q: An invoice check paid === due fails because 1.1 + 2.2 is 3.3000000000000003. Why is changing it to paid >= due not a real fix?
questions.explain: 0.7 + 0.1 is 0.7999999999999999, which is less than 0.8. The error's direction depends on the numbers, so >= only works by luck. Store whole kobo instead.
options: Because >= does not work on decimals
Because for other amounts the rounding error goes the other way, and a fully paid invoice would come out slightly short

questions.q: What removes the root cause of wrong comparisons on money amounts?
questions.explain: Whole numbers are stored exactly, so sums of kobo are exact and === works. Decimals are converted only for display.
options: Rounding with toFixed(2) and comparing the strings
Storing and adding amounts as whole kobo, which are exact
Adding the payments in a different order

questions.q: A cart function writes total = item.price * item.quantity instead of adding to the total. Which test would not catch this?
questions.explain: With one item, replacing and adding give the same answer. You need at least two items to see that earlier items are thrown away, which is why "one item" and "several items" are separate edge cases.
options: A cart with exactly one item
A cart where the last item is cheaper than the first

questions.q: How do you know you have really found and fixed a bug?
questions.explain: The failing test proves your explanation matches the program's behaviour, and it keeps the bug from coming back unnoticed. If you cannot make a test fail before your fix, you have not found the bug yet.
options: You can explain the cause, and you have a test that fails on the old code and passes on the new code

questions.q: A total prints as NaN. Which suspect should you check first?
questions.explain: NaN is what arithmetic produces from undefined or non-numeric text, and it spreads to every later result. Loop bounds and starting values are the usual culprits.
options: A condition in the wrong order
Something undefined (or text) getting into the arithmetic: reading past a list, or a counter with no starting value

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The loop makes one step too many. kobo[3] does not exist, so it is undefined, and 3000 + undefined is NaN.

questions.explain: The loop starts at 1 because best already holds position 0. At i=2, 2 is not bigger than 7, so best stays 7. Starting at 1 is correct here, because the first item was used as the starting value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 90,000 is at least 1,000, so the first check returns 25 and the ₦50 rule is never reached. The broader check must come after the more specific one.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: At i=1 the first "cancel" is removed and the second slides into position 1, which is skipped. At i=2 the third "cancel" (now there) is removed. The middle one survives.

questions.q: The same removal, walking backwards. What does it print?
questions.explain: Walking from the end, a removal only shifts items the loop has already visited, so nothing is skipped. All three cancellations are removed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0.1 * 3 is 0.30000000000000004, so exact comparison fails. Whole numbers (think kobo) are exact. Comparing with a tolerance accepts the tiny error.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each step replaces the total, so only the last line counts. With one line the answer happens to be right (600), which is why a one-item test cannot catch this bug.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both branches return, so only the first invoice is ever looked at. An empty list never enters the loop and the function ends without return, giving undefined.

questions.q: A safety counter stops this recursion after 6 calls. What does it print?
questions.explain: 4, 2, 0 reaches the base case. 5, 3, 1, −1, −3, … steps over 0 and only the safety counter stops it. n <= 0 would be reachable from both.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For an empty list the loop never runs, so the function computes 0 / 0, which is NaN. The empty list needs its own decision, such as returning null.

questions.q: This loop pays off a ₦10,000 debt in ₦3,000 instalments. What does it print?
questions.explain: After 3 months ₦1,000 is still owed, so a 4th month runs. The last instalment overpays by ₦2,000: the loop needs the rule "the last payment is only what is left", or the lender refunds ₦2,000.

questions.q: This function should add up the last 3 values of a list, or all of them if there are fewer than 3. It has an off-by-one bug and does not handle short lists. Fix it.
questions.explain: < stops at the last real position, and Math.max(0, …) keeps the start from going below 0 for short lists. An empty list adds nothing: 0.

questions.q: Fix the order of the checks: parcels over 10 kg cost ₦5,000, over 1 kg cost ₦1,500, anything else heavier than 0 costs ₦800, and 0 or less is "invalid".
questions.explain: The most specific check (over 10 kg) must come first, or the "over 1 kg" check catches every heavy parcel. The tests sit on both sides of each boundary: 1 and 4, 10 and 12.

questions.q: Add a base case so that sumTo(n) returns 1 + 2 + … + n, and returns 0 for any n of 0 or less, so every input stops.
questions.explain: n <= 0 is reachable from every number, including negatives, unlike n === 0. 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10.

questions.q: The function below removes expired coupons with splice in a forward loop and misses some. Rewrite it so it returns a new list of the coupons that are not expired, leaving the input unchanged.
questions.explain: Building a new list means the loop never walks over a list that is changing, so nothing is skipped, and the caller's list still has all 3 coupons.

questions.q: Instalments are recorded in naira with decimals, and isPaid fails for ₦0.70 + ₦0.10 against ₦0.80. Fix it by converting every amount to whole kobo (Math.round(naira * 100)) before adding and comparing.
questions.explain: Each amount is turned into a whole number of kobo, and sums of whole numbers are exact. Math.round removes the tiny error in p * 100 itself. The last test checks that an underpaid invoice is still reported as unpaid.

questions.q: This function should say whether any task is overdue, but it only looks at the first task. Fix it: return true as soon as one overdue task is found, and false only after checking them all.
questions.explain: "Any" can answer yes early, but can only answer no after seeing every task. The return false belongs after the loop, which also gives an empty list a real answer instead of undefined.

questions.q: Fix totalHours so it adds up the hours of every timesheet entry instead of returning only the last one.
questions.explain: Each step must add to the running total: total = total + entry.hours. The one-entry test passed even before the fix; the three-entry test is the one that exposes the bug.

questions.q: Reorder the checks so that canWithdraw(null, 500) returns "no: not logged in" instead of crashing.
questions.explain: The null check protects every later line that reads account.something, so it has to come first.
questions.expected:
yes
no: account frozen
no: not logged in
